works.title: Replicability
Bilimsel Kriterler Işığında İki Psikoloji: Klasik Dönem Psikolojisi ile Modern Psikoloji (1800–1960) Arasındaki Metodolojik, Epistemolojik ve Tekrarlanabilirlik Karşılaştırması
works.abstract: Bu çalışma, milattan önce 4. yüzyıldan milat sonra 17. yüzyıla uzanan klasik dönem psikolojisi ile 1800-1960 yılları arasında kurumlaşan modern Batı psikolojisini; tekrarlanabilirlik, yanlışlanabilirlik, veri toplama yöntemleri, örneklem geçerliliği, epistemolojik çerçeve ve etik standartlar gibi bilimsel kriterler açısından sistematik biçimde karşılaştırmaktadır. Çalışma; modern psikolojinin kendini bilimsel olarak diğer dönemlerden üstün konumlandırma iddiasını, replikasyon krizi ve WEIRD örneklem sorunu gibi bulgular ışığında eleştirel biçimde değerlendirmektedir. Klasik dönemin metodolojik sınırlılıklarını teslim ederken, modern dönemin de yapısal sorunlarını göz ardı etmediğini; her iki dönemin de insana ilişkin bilgiye farklı ama eşit derecede meşru kanallardan ulaştığını savunmaktadır. Karşılaştırmalı tablo analizleri, vaka örnekleri ve 2015 replikasyon krizinin bulguları bu savı desteklemek için kullanılmaktadır.

works.title: 6 Behavioural Science Will Replicate
Volume III: Empirical Generalizations and Meta-Analysis. Don Lehman’s Contributions to Understanding Empirical Generalization Through Meta-Analysis
Behave well in someone else's place! Genderization of urban spaces influences environmental behavior in public settings
works.abstract: Gender differences in environmental behavior are well-documented, yet research has largely overlooked how behaviors can be influenced by social meanings attributed to physical space. Urban spaces are inherently imbued with gendered traits, a concept grounded in feminist geography theory and supported by recent findings on space-focused stereotyping processes. Building on this evidence, Study 1 (N = 130) revealed the influence of gendered urban space perceptions on social expectations regarding gender differences in environmental behavior. Study 2 (N = 170) replicated these findings using a Gender Face Recognition Task indirectly measuring the cognitive association between masculinity and urban environments. Study 3 (N = 204) experimentally manipulated the cognitive accessibility of (counter-)stereotypical beliefs about urban spaces. Despite a manipulation backfire effect, results highlighted gender role norms as a mechanism influencing the gendering of environmental behaviors in public settings. Across studies, stereotypical beliefs about urban spaces and gender roles help explain gender gaps in environmentalism. We discuss implications for socio-environmental psychology and for urban designs that acknowledge gender dynamics to promote inclusive, sustainable public spaces.

works.title: The Bayesian audit: evaluating the proportionality of scientific claims to evidence — a case study on social priming and walking speed
works.abstract: Across psychology, bold empirical claims often outpace the evidential support on which they rest. The replication crisis has shown that statistical significance alone provides little guidance about what should rationally be believed. To address this gap between results and rhetoric, we introduce the Bayesian audit-a conceptual and normative framework, rather than a new statistical method, for evaluating whether scientific claims are proportionate to the strength of their evidence. The audit proceeds by identifying the claim, specifying priors, translating the empirical evidence into a likelihood-based measure, updating to obtain posterior belief, testing sensitivity, and synthesizing proportional conclusions. Applied to a well-known case in social psychology-the "elderly priming" study by Bargh et al. (1996)-the audit reveals that the original finding corresponds to only modest Bayesian evidence (Bayes factor ≈ 3). Under reasonable priors (0.05-0.20), the posterior probability that the effect is genuine remains below 0.5, and replication attempts provide limited additional evidential impact at the level of individual studies. The exercise illustrates how strong theoretical language can emerge from weak evidential shifts and how Bayesian reasoning can realign scientific communication with inferential logic. The framework is particularly relevant for psychological science, where replication failures often reflect over-claiming rather than data absence, and where proportional reasoning can help restore coherence between evidence and belief.

works.title: The Replication Crisis in Psychology
works.abstract: The replication crisis in psychology is often framed as a methodological failure—an issue of flawed statistical practices, publication bias, and poor experimental design. While these factors undoubtedly play a role, this article argues that the replication crisis is much more than a methodological problem. Psychology’s struggle with replication is not merely a consequence of weak methodologies but a reflection of deeper epistemological, theoretical, historical, political, and institutional challenges within the discipline. In this article, I present five reasons why the replication crisis should be understood as more than just a crisis of methods.

works.title: The Virtues of Lab Experiments
works.abstract: Physical laboratory experiments occupy a key position within experimental economics for a wide range of research questions, offering crucial methodological rigor by ensuring human authenticity, controlling informational conditions, directing interpersonal interactions, ensuring protocol credibility, and reliably administering monetary incentives. These factors contribute to the empirical robustness of experimental findings. The continued advancement of online experimental platforms offers complementary scientific benefits to laboratory experiments, such as lowering costs and increasing sample diversity. We identify and elaborate on specific research questions for which laboratory-based methods offer clear scientific advantages, emphasizing their ability to yield precise, insightful, and replicable data.

works.title: How the Unconscious Thinks
works.abstract: Chapter 5 examines research on unconscious mental states and processes, starting with the emergence of the ‘cognitive unconscious’ during the 1990s. The chapter reviews the developments of doubts about initial claims regarding implicit perceptions and attitudes, particularly the ability of implicit attitude measures to tap unconscious prejudices. It covers the troubled history of how social priming research became one of the prominent examples of the replication crisis in psychology. Its central focus is on debates about the extent to which automaticity and unconscious biases dominate judgements and decisions, to the detriment of autonomy. The setting for these debates is the emergence of ‘dual systems’ models of cognition, wherein ‘System 1’ operates automatically and quickly while ‘System 2’ operates in a deliberative style and with a sense of voluntary control. Chapter 5 concludes with a brief overview of lay beliefs about how the unconscious thinks.

works.title: Space oddity: How context matters in waste-sorting behavior
works.venue: Recherche et Applications en Marketing (English Edition)
works.abstract: The circular economy gives a prominent role to recycling, entailing the general implementation of waste sorting in private, semi-public, and public locations. Previous literature has extensively explored the psychological and contextual antecedents of waste-sorting behavior, but mainly with a focus on one specific setting, without considering how the sorting location might moderate the influence of these antecedents. To investigate this research question, we develop a dual-route model of waste-sorting behavior based on an integrated TPB-NAM framework. To test this model, we used a survey based on self-reported data considering three successive locations (i.e. home, university, and on the way to university) from the same 296 French college students and analyzed it using structural equation modeling with partial least squares (PLS-SEM). Although both psychological and contextual routes influence waste sorting, we show that their relative importance differs across locations. Furthermore, at university and on the way to university, the contextual route influences the psychological one. These results highlight why individuals’ self-reported waste-sorting behavior may vary across locations and call on academics to replicate pro-environmental behavior models across all relevant contexts before recommending public policies to promote them.

works.title: Social Psychology’s Empty-Self Metaphor and the Replication Crisis
works.abstract: Since the early 20th century, an emphasis on the causal power of situations in social psychology has fostered the view that the self is an empty vessel filled by the contents of the situation. We label this the "empty-self metaphor," with incarnations including situationism and elements of theories of self-presentation, self-perception, social identity, the dramaturgical movement, and others. The persistence of this metatheoretical assumption has led to an underappreciation of an enduring, unique self and to the development of contemporary paradigms (e.g., social priming and embodied cognition) that have hinged on the implicit premise that the self is empty or passive. The self is not empty, of course, and new preliminary evidence we have collected indicates that research predicated on the empty-self metaphor is far less likely to replicate. Although we emphasize that the power of the situation has yielded important theoretical and practical insights, we propose that the field would be strengthened by better accounting for the chronic, dispositional motivations that emanate from an enduring self. We offer suggestions-both theoretical and methodological-that can help social psychologists achieve this goal.

works.title: Beyond Algorithmic Transparency: Behavioral Administrative Burdens, Contestability, and Citizen Trust in AI-Assisted Public Decisions
works.abstract: Public authorities increasingly deploy artificial intelligence (AI) to classify applications, prioritize caseloads, and support decisions affecting access to public services. Yet formal transparency does not establish that affected individuals understand a decision, recognize a possible error, or can exercise review rights. This article develops a behavioral-economic account of effective contestability in AI-assisted public administration, integrating bounded rationality, administrative burden, procedural justice, and algorithmic reliance. We distinguish information about a decision from citizens’ practical ability to convert that information into corrective action. The proposed contestability-conversion framework models an applicant’s decision to challenge as a function of expected correction, perceived legitimacy, cognitive and emotional costs, and the friction of procedural steps. Building on relevant Italian legal scholarship, we specify a prospective, ethically constrained 2 × 2 × 2 factorial field experiment varying comprehensible explanation, actionable guidance, and administrative friction reduction, while preserving all statutory rights and mandatory notices. We identify primary and secondary outcomes, independent error adjudication, preregistered estimands, heterogeneous treatment effects, multiplicity controls, data-protection safeguards, and competing mechanisms. Rather than claiming unobserved results, the article explains which causal contrasts could establish whether a communication intervention changes comprehension, appropriately targeted challenges, correction of errors, or trust. We argue that public-sector behavioral policy should assess both beneficial and unnecessary appeals, distributional consequences, caseworker workloads, and the legitimacy of the underlying decision procedure. The resulting framework links explainable AI to observable procedural capability and offers a replicable evaluation strategy for accountable public institutions. Its central criterion is procedurally meaningful correction rather than indiscriminate engagement.

works.title: Quantifying the factors behind the decision to produce second-generation ethanol in Brazil: a Fuzzy-QFD decision-support model.
works.abstract: Second-generation (2G) ethanol is a strategic route for decarbonizing the energy matrix through lignocellulosic residues, yet its consolidation in Brazil remains limited and the corporate decision to produce it is poorly understood quantitatively. To address this gap, this study develops and applies a Fuzzy Quality Function Deployment (Fuzzy-QFD) decision-support model that quantifies how strongly each factor and barrier is weighed in the decision to produce 2G ethanol, and how this weighting differs among production-system actors. Nine critical factors and twelve expected-quality groups were derived from two systematic reviews and structured as a House of Quality; linguistic judgments from 40 stakeholders spanning the Triple Helix (industry, academia, and government) were encoded as triangular fuzzy numbers, aggregated (with competence-based coefficients applied to the correlation judgments), and defuzzified into crisp values that populated the matrix. The analysis is framed by the Triple Bottom Line and the Sustainable Development Goals. Industrial Efficiency ranked first (about 11% of relative importance), indicating that 2G ethanol is treated as a commodity whose competitiveness depends on process optimization rather than product properties, while Technology emerged as the structural driver of the model. Although Environmental Sustainability shared the highest declared importance with Technology, it showed limited operational influence, suggesting a gap between sustainability commitments and their translation into decision-making, with implications for SDG 13. The priorities are associative rather than causal and reflect the evaluated stakeholders, part of whom validated document-informed drafts. The model provides a replicable tool that converts subjective judgments into impact coefficients for each decision actor.

works.title: RagHarnessDebugger: Jev-Guided Agentic RAG in Contract Inference Repair Auditing
works.abstract: Agentic systems using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) must repair their own answers by gathering more evidence, testing alternative policies and deciding if, when, and what repairs are needed. Yet how do we know if a system's repairs are working when metrics like accuracy can be misleading? We present RagHarnessDebugger, a framework that records every repair decision in a Jev-guided harness for contract inference and audits the record to facilitate complete debugging of all decisions taken during a RAG repair journey. RagHarnessDebugger checks that each trace is intact, that each validation applies to the candidate it is counted for, and which answers the acceptance rule can reach. We tested our approach on ContractNLI non-disclosure agreements with two reader models and a replication set of separate contracts. Our debugger's audit layer exposed failure patterns that were hidden under aggregate metrics, policies acceptance cost of repairs vs regressions and policy acceptance gap of 77% and 76% of available but unrealised repairs on development and replication sets. Our audit, together with a labeled error analysis and replay mechanism, allowed following the execution path all the way to the terminal decision - uncovering where missing repairs became lost. Our revised harness improved accuracy over the initial BM25-only baseline by 3.6 points on development contracts and 3.7 points on the replication set, and even improved our full contract access reference score by 1.1 on development and 2.4 on replication set. While our work here demonstrates how the debugger can conduct decision root-cause analysis for missed repairs, the true value lies with providing this debugger for judgment visibility serving continuous improvement of RAG decisions and their explainability. Keywords: agentic RAG, AI evidence repair, harness explainability, counterfactual replay, Jev, ContractNLI

works.title: Framing, Anchoring and Decoy Effects in AI-Mediated Heritage Tourism: A Behavioral Economics Audit of Large Language Models
works.abstract: Tourists increasingly consult large language models (LLMs) for heritage tourism decisions, making these systems new choice architects. This study audits four Claude models (Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1) acting as travel advisors for framing, anchoring, and decoy effects. Market-calibrated scenarios on a heritage conservation donation in Cappadocia, a guided-tour price in Istanbul’s Historic Peninsula, and a tour-package choice in Nicosia were administered in two wording versions in independent sessions (N = 280), complemented by four supplementary experiments testing design confounds (N = 440). The loss frame did not increase donations but raised the share of rationales criticizing the message from 2.5% to 55%. The larger models’ price estimates shifted in both directions toward reference prices, even toward prices they explicitly rejected in their rationales. A decoy package raised the probability of recommending the community-based package by 22.5 percentage points in the main study and in a recalibrated replication; the effect was in the same direction when option order was counterbalanced and when the decoy carried a neutral name. The baseline obtained with the same prompt changed markedly within three weeks. The findings show that specific model versions respond systematically to specific choice architectures and that these responses vary by model, wording, and time; AI-mediated channels should therefore be audited regularly, with version and date records.

works.title: Behavioural Biases in Conventional and Sustainable Investment Decisions in Emerging Markets: A Bibliometric and Systematic Review with a Research Agenda
works.venue: Journal of risk and financial management
works.abstract: This study maps and synthesises research on behavioural biases and investor decision-making in emerging markets, including sustainable investing, to identify the field’s structure, the consistency of its evidence and its gaps. Following PRISMA 2020, three Scopus search strings (2010–2026) returned 1037 unique records, which were screened against six pre-defined criteria, including a uniform requirement that the empirical setting be an emerging or developing market. The 399 eligible documents were analysed bibliometrically (performance analysis, construct co-occurrence and thematic mapping), and the 386 empirical studies among them were coded with a structured extraction form, appraised for methodological quality and synthesised without meta-analysis by vote counting of effect directions, with sign tests, sensitivity analyses and GRADE-adapted certainty ratings. Output grew by 27.1% a year (2011–2025) and is concentrated in India, China, Indonesia and Pakistan, while GCC markets are the setting of 4.3% of documents. Of 328 bias–outcome associations reported by 152 individual-investor studies, 62.5% use generic self-reported “investment decision” scales and 41.5% are reported without a direction of effect. The most consistent findings are that overconfidence is associated with more trading activity (10 of 10 studies reporting a direction; low certainty) and that market-wide herding is conditional on down markets and crises (unconditional in seven of 26 tests; moderate certainty). Mediation by risk perception rests on 17 cross-sectional surveys concentrated in South Asia (low certainty), herding is inconsistently related to individual decisions, and financial literacy is associated with fewer cognitive biases but not with less overconfidence. Research should prioritise behavioural outcome data, measures of decision quality and multi-country designs before these mechanisms are treated as established.

works.title: From decision support to continuous improvement: GenAI appropriation, performance and self-assessment calibration
works.abstract: Purpose This study investigates how different modes of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) appropriation are associated with two complementary dimensions of continuous improvement in decision-making. The first is decision-making performance, which reflects the cognitive ability to make effective choices; the second is pre-feedback self-assessment calibration, which captures the metacognitive ability to align perceived decision quality with objective outcomes across iterative decision-making cycles. Design/methodology/approach The study involved 36 managers from manufacturing companies enrolled in lean six sigma green belt courses. To assess decision-making performance over time, a multi-round business simulation game designed to replicate complex decision-making scenarios was employed. At the end of each simulation round, participants completed a questionnaire measuring their ability to self-assess the quality of their decisions. Semi-structured interviews were also conducted to examine how participants interacted with GenAI. Findings The results indicate that different modes of GenAI appropriation are associated with distinct trajectories of decision-making performance and self-assessment calibration. Reflective use of the technology was associated with higher decision-making performance and greater improvement in self-assessment calibration. Passive use, characterised by a high level of delegation of decision-making to GenAI, was associated with more volatile performance trajectories and poorer calibration. Progressively reflective use was associated with intermediate but improving trajectories over time. Originality/value This study introduces a longitudinal perspective on GenAI-supported decision-making by jointly examining decision-making performance and pre-feedback self-assessment calibration across repeated decision cycles. By relating different appropriation modes to cognitive and metacognitive trajectories, this study extends research beyond approaches focused on isolated performance outcomes and provides a process-oriented view of decision-making improvement over time.

works.title: Studies of AI-based Expert Decision-Making in Planning and Forecasting for Warranty Extension Management
works.abstract: Effective organizational decision-making in individual and group settings requires decision-makers to integrate diverse decision attributes into coherent outcomes. While human expertise remains an essential advisory source to decision-makers, it is constrained by cognitive limitations such as limited information-processing capacity and bias. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) have introduced intelligent agents capable of large-scale data processing and pattern recognition beyond human capacity. However, ML systems represent a different, rather than superior, form of reasoning: they excel at data-intensive analysis but lack contextual understanding and evaluative judgment. Consequently, sole reliance on ML-based advice is insufficient for many organizational decision contexts, as these inherently depend on contextual factors and nuanced human judgment. Combining human and ML-based advice offers the potential to leverage complementary strengths and mitigate respective limitations, enabling decision-makers to achieve more reliable decision outcomes. Yet, despite increasing organizational adoption of intelligent agents, existing research largely focuses on single-advisor or static decision-support scenarios, providing limited insight into how decision-makers engage with multiple advisory sources in both individual and group contexts. As a result, the design, use, and effects of human–ML ensembles in organizational decision-making remain insufficiently understood. This dissertation addresses this gap by exploring the design of information systems that facilitate human–ML ensemble-advised decision-making. Grounded in Design Science Research, it adopts a multi-layered enterprise architecture perspective, comprising the technology, application, and business process levels, to provide a holistic framework for integrating human and ML advice effectively. At the technology level, the dissertation develops design knowledge on AI-based advisory mechanisms that serve as reliable contributors within human–ML ensembles rather than opaque automation tools. To this end, robo-advisor platforms, originally developed to guide investors through automated investment advisory processes in asset and wealth management, were analyzed and identified as a promising technological foundation for structuring advisory processes that support decision-making across the phases of a typical decision process. Paper A synthesizes 14 years of robo-advisor research in a structured literature review examining existing robo-advisory design requirements and recommendations, which served as a foundation for the subsequent application- and process-level analyses. In parallel, Paper B presents a preliminary Design Science Research project exploring the application of robo-advisory concepts to novel organizational decision-making contexts and extending their application beyond traditional asset and wealth management scenarios. These technological insights lay the foundation for the subsequent application- and process-level investigations. At the application level, the dissertation provides design guidance on integrating heterogeneous advisory inputs from human experts and ML systems. Insights from the VDI Report (Paper C) on the use of robo-advisory and AI in reliability analysis for field measure decision-making informed on key tasks within the advisory process on the platform. Paper D presents the prototypical instantiation of the robo-advisor, adapted to support group decision-making, which generates context-specific design knowledge relevant to enterprise financial planning. These application-level insights guide practitioners in shaping reflective and critical advice-taking behaviors, reducing risks of blind delegation or uncritical reliance, and operationalizing ensemble advice to enhance decision quality across multiple contexts. These design principles inform the structuring of organizational processes to enable effective ensemble decision-making, as explored

works.title: The Allure of Simplicity: Framing Effects and Theoretical Virtues
works.abstract: Are simpler explanations better, all else equal? Many people seem to think so. And many capitalize on this preference by claiming that their explanations are simple-perhaps the simplest! But some scholars have argued that the case for simplicity's status as a theoretical virtue is quite thin. And some psychological studies raise questions about the reliability of simplicity's benefits. Alas, once acquired, status as a theoretical virtue is rarely lost. To advance the debate, we conducted three experiments that test another way so-called theoretical virtues may impact reasoning (N = 1312). Merely labeling diagnoses "the simplest explanation" made them more alluring in ways that were not warranted by relevant base rates, symptoms, or other causal information (experiment 1)-even when those diagnoses were not actually the simplest! Neither the opposite label ("most complex") nor an alternative explanatory virtue label ("most unifying") had such consistent or reliable effects (experiment 2), suggesting simplicity itself is particularly seductive. The good news is that judgments and decisions were mostly unaffected by fallacious appeals to simplicity when we switched to other contexts and measures (experiment 3). That limited generalization suggests a variety of testable hypotheses about the boundaries and moderators of simplicity's allure. For example, perhaps people rely more on intuitions about simplicity when diagnostic decision-making would otherwise require effortful reflection on technical terminology and difficult-to-compute probabilities. Together, our findings replicate and extend prior research on simplicity preferences, complement recent arguments and evidence about the risk of considering simplicity, and increase suspicion about simplicity's virtuous status.

works.title: STRESS-TESTING FIXED EFFECTS: A MONTE CARLO EVALUATION OF A TWO-WAY FIXEDEFFECTS FRAMEWORK FOR COGNITIVE OVERRELIANCE IN HUMAN-AI COLLABORATION
works.abstract: Predictive AI systems are increasingly embedded in tasks once reserved for expert judgment, raising a question for information systems research: Does algorithmic assistance sharpen professional judgment, or erode it? Before committing to a longitudinal registry study, this paper asks a logically prior question: does the identification strategy such a study would use actually work, and under what conditions would it fail? We construct a synthetic panel of 50 experts evaluating 40 cases across four periods (2,000 observations per replication), embedding a known relationship among algorithmic reliance, decision variation, and diagnostic error. Across 500 Monte Carlo replications, a two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) framework recovers the built-in decision-homogenization effect and U-shaped reliance-error relationship with low bias and near-nominal coverage. We then extend this baseline in two ways. First, comparing TWFE against pooled OLS under independent and confounded data-generating processes shows that pooled OLS is essentially unbiased in the first case and biased by roughly 52% in the second, while TWFE remains unbiased in both cases, clarifying precisely when the fixed-effects correction does identifying work instead of improving precision. Second, stress-testing the estimating equation against four departures from its baseline assumptions, a kinked threshold relationship, heterogeneous reliance slopes, a logistic error process, and reliance that responds dynamically to past errors, shows the pipeline remains well-calibrated under slope heterogeneity, but that coverage and the power of the Lind-Mehlum U-shape test both deteriorate markedly under a logistic error process and dynamic feedback. All results describe estimator behavior under a known synthetic data-generating process; they are not empirical claims about real professionals.

works.title: Risk perception, institutional trust and misinformation as correlates of public avoidance behaviour in South Korea following the Fukushima treated-water discharge: implications for radiological protection communication
works.abstract: Public avoidance behaviour following radiological events can persist even when authoritative assessments judge the associated exposure to be negligible, posing a persistent challenge for radiological protection communication. Taking Japan's discharge of Advanced Liquid Processing System-treated water from the Fukushima Daiichi site into the Pacific Ocean as a case, this study asks why comparable levels of perceived risk are associated with avoidance behaviour for some individuals but not for others. Drawing on risk perception theory, the trust literature and dual-process models of information processing, we examine how nuclear risk perception, institutional trust, factual knowledge, acceptance of misinformation and modes of information processing shape whether people avoid Japanese seafood and products, forgo travel to Japan and discourage others from travelling. Using survey data from a quota sample of 1898 South Korean adults, we estimate hierarchical and moderated regression models of avoidance behaviour. Risk perception was the strongest predictor and established the baseline impulse to avoid, with event-specific accident risk perception exerting a stronger effect than general nuclear risk perception. Institutional trust was associated with lower avoidance and misinformation acceptance with higher avoidance, while the two knowledge measures operated in opposing directions. Systematic and heuristic processing further conditioned the influence of trust, household income and risk perception, indicating that these factors are associated with the strength of the perception-behaviour relationship rather than acting as interchangeable predictors. For radiological protection, the results suggest that communication addressing affective risk perceptions, sustained trust-building and active countering of misinformation, tailored to how audiences process information, may be more effective than technical reassurance alone in managing public responses to contested exposure situations. Treating trust, misinformation and information processing as conditions on the perception-behaviour relationship offers a testable basis for anticipating when public response and technical assessment diverge. Because the design is cross-sectional, all estimates reported here are associations rather than causal effects, and because the sample is drawn from a single national public that is geographically distant from the discharge site, generalisation beyond South Korea requires comparative replication.

works.title: Does the Outfit Change the Price? Context Halo in Vision-Language Model Valuation of an Identical Low-Cost Necklace
works.abstract: A chunky gold-tone chain necklace bought online for 2.43 USD was photographed four ways: worn with formal attire against a wood-panelled wall, worn at a party, worn with casual clothing in a recycling yard, and laid flat with no person present. We asked six frontier language models to estimate its price in 1,164 independent and sequential API sessions (4,604 logged rows) and compared estimates across settings. Among the four models that answered image prompts, the same necklace was priced 1.9 to 3.3 times higher in the formal photograph than in the flat-lay (all p < 0.01). Against the yard photograph, the ratio ranged from 1.23 (Grok 4.5, not significant) to 3.57 (Kimi K3), with Claude Fable 5 at 3.32. A text-only version of the task, in which the setting is described in words, produced formal-to-yard ratios of 2.2 to 3.9 in all six models, so the effect does not require pixels. Flat-lay estimates themselves were 7.8 to 18.7 times the receipt price, so part of any headline "outfit multiplier" computed against the receipt is baseline overestimate, not a context effect. A single instruction to ignore clothing and setting significantly reduced the effect in one model (ratio of ratios 0.77, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.91) and not detectably in the others; telling the model the photo came from a company website or a personal account changed nothing significant. Asked afterward whether a different outfit would have changed their number, Claude Fable 5 said yes in 24 of 24 sessions, GPT-5.6 in 69%, and GPT-4o in 18%, while GPT-4o also refused 79% of image estimation prompts. The study isolates a mechanism with one object and one wearer at about 10 sessions per model and condition; we outline the replication needed next, with multiple objects and a human benchmark. Data, code, and raw outputs are released.

works.title: Quantitative Reliability Analysis of Mitigations Against Construction-Stage Wetting of Cross Laminated Timber Roof Structures
works.abstract: The built environment produces about one third of global CO₂ emissions, making rapid decarbonisation essential. Timber buildings could significantly reduce these emissions, yet recent failures caused by moisture intrusion during construction have led to timber decay. Despite broad recognition of the issue, designers and contractors lack quantitative guidance, relying instead on incomplete and anecdotal recommendations. Real construction projects are too complex to replicate in laboratories, creating a shortage of scientific evidence, while valuable industry knowledge remains fragmented and underused. This study introduces a structured expert‑elicitation method that weights expert opinions by calibration performance. A panel of leading industry experts evaluated 19 commonly recommended construction‑stage moisture mitigation strategies. The method offers greater rigour, accuracy, and transparency than standard surveys. Results show, for the first time, that several widely endorsed measures perform poorly in practice or impose major design, cost, or time burdens. The findings provide new evidence to improve design guidance and strengthen moisture‑risk decision‑making through objective identification of effective mitigation strategies. This will support more reliable outcomes and help ensure the safe expansion of timber construction as part of broader decarbonisation efforts.

works.title: Quality Controls Can Improve the Replicability of Survey Experiments Using Online Nonprobability Panels
works.abstract: Scholars across multiple disciplines have documented challenges related to replicability, often referred to as a “replication crisis.” While a range of explanations exist, some have argued that the growing reliance on online nonprobability samples contributes to replication failures. At the same time, concerns have mounted regarding the quality of these samples, as inattentive, duplicate, or fraudulent respondents can bias estimates and diminish effect sizes. In this research note, we replicate three well-known survey experiments, using data collected from three separate online nonprobability panels (N = 6,000). We compare the “off-the-shelf” samples with subsets that pass a series of attention and fraud checks and that remove duplicate respondents. We find that all three experiments replicate in terms of direction and significance across the full samples, but in two out of three cases, effect magnitudes are replicated only once low-quality responses are removed.

works.title: Framing, Anchoring and Decoy Effects in AI-Mediated Heritage Tourism: A Behavioral Economics Audit of Large Language Models
works.abstract: Tourists increasingly consult large language models (LLMs) for heritage tourism decisions, making these systems new choice architects. This study audits four Claude models (Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1) acting as travel advisors for framing, anchoring, and decoy effects. Market-calibrated scenarios on a heritage conservation donation in Cappadocia, a guided-tour price in Istanbul’s Historic Peninsula, and a tour-package choice in Nicosia were administered in two wording versions in independent sessions (N = 280), complemented by four supplementary experiments testing design confounds (N = 440). The loss frame did not increase donations but raised the share of rationales criticizing the message from 2.5% to 55%. The larger models’ price estimates shifted in both directions toward reference prices, even toward prices they explicitly rejected in their rationales. A decoy package raised the probability of recommending the community-based package by 22.5 percentage points in the main study and in a recalibrated replication; the effect was in the same direction when option order was counterbalanced and when the decoy carried a neutral name. The baseline obtained with the same prompt changed markedly within three weeks. The findings show that specific model versions respond systematically to specific choice architectures and that these responses vary by model, wording, and time; AI-mediated channels should therefore be audited regularly, with version and date records.

works.title: The Allure of Simplicity: Framing Effects and Theoretical Virtues
works.abstract: Are simpler explanations better, all else equal? Many people seem to think so. And many capitalize on this preference by claiming that their explanations are simple-perhaps the simplest! But some scholars have argued that the case for simplicity's status as a theoretical virtue is quite thin. And some psychological studies raise questions about the reliability of simplicity's benefits. Alas, once acquired, status as a theoretical virtue is rarely lost. To advance the debate, we conducted three experiments that test another way so-called theoretical virtues may impact reasoning (N = 1312). Merely labeling diagnoses "the simplest explanation" made them more alluring in ways that were not warranted by relevant base rates, symptoms, or other causal information (experiment 1)-even when those diagnoses were not actually the simplest! Neither the opposite label ("most complex") nor an alternative explanatory virtue label ("most unifying") had such consistent or reliable effects (experiment 2), suggesting simplicity itself is particularly seductive. The good news is that judgments and decisions were mostly unaffected by fallacious appeals to simplicity when we switched to other contexts and measures (experiment 3). That limited generalization suggests a variety of testable hypotheses about the boundaries and moderators of simplicity's allure. For example, perhaps people rely more on intuitions about simplicity when diagnostic decision-making would otherwise require effortful reflection on technical terminology and difficult-to-compute probabilities. Together, our findings replicate and extend prior research on simplicity preferences, complement recent arguments and evidence about the risk of considering simplicity, and increase suspicion about simplicity's virtuous status.

works.title: Bridging Perceptual and Value Signal Evaluation: Meta‐Analytic Evidence for the Claustrum as a Cross‐Domain Integrator in Decision‐Making
works.abstract: Decision-making requires evaluating information across both perceptual and value domains, yet the neural mechanisms supporting this cross-domain convergence remain unclear. Using activation likelihood estimation (ALE) and meta-analytic connectivity modeling (MACM), we conducted a large-scale cross-domain meta-analysis of 90 fMRI studies involving 2564 participants to examine the neural correlates of perceptual and value signal evaluation. The results revealed partially segregated yet overlapping neural architectures for perceptual and value signal evaluation. Perceptual signal evaluation was primarily associated with a dorsal fronto-parietal-visual system, whereas value signal evaluation was mainly associated with a striato-thalamo-cingulate system. Importantly, the conjunction analysis identified the bilateral claustrum and left medial frontal gyrus as shared convergence regions across domains. MACM further showed distinguishable coactivation profiles, suggesting that these shared regions may participate in coordinating domain-specific perceptual and value-related networks rather than forming a single common decision system. Together, these findings support the claustrum as a candidate domain-general integrator that may bridge sensory, motivational, and executive processes, providing a cross-domain account of decision-making.

works.title: Calibrating risk perception in household food safety: A mixed-methods field trial of framing and regulatory fit
The Influence of Negative Language on Decision-Making
works.venue: Lecture Notes in Education Psychology and Public Media
works.abstract: Negative Language may affect people's choices in daily life through two distinct routes: linguistic negation, which is the linguistic polarity of lexicalisation, and negative framing, which focuses on losses or undesirable outcomes. This paper studies how linguistic negation affects pre-decision states and changes the final choice of the negative frame according to cognitive and biological evidence. Based on the prior studies discussed in Section A, linguistic negation increases the cognitive load and reduces decision efficiency. Results of stop-signal tasks indicate that the cognitive resources required for negation processing overlap with those needed for inhibitory control, and event-related potential data have linked negation to delayed semantic reanalysis and integration. Surveys, bilingual and risk-choice studies in Section B have shown that negative framing can change people's judgments of objectively equivalent options in many languages, tasks and people. Neuroimaging studies have identified brain areas involved in gain- and loss-domain framing, and stimulation of the ventromedial prefrontal cortex shows that it regulates these decisions to be more rational. In short, the paper does not hold that negative language has a single or always harmful effect on decision-making. The scope of the negativity and the level of decision-making will affect how much of it is revealed.

works.title: The Use and Usefulness of Corporate Sustainability Information
works.abstract: Sustainability disclosures are more common than ever. Yet whether they are actually useful remains an open question. This dissertation examines that question across three studies spanning different audiences, methods, and sustainability domains.The first study systematically reviews how business journal articles engage with third-party sustainability measures in sustainability-financial performance linking research. The review identifies two sources of uncertainty that limit confidence in these measures: the quality of underlying data and how data is aggregated. Methodological rigor is bimodal; researchers either scrutinize multiple dimensions of measurement quality or none at all, and choices about data quality and aggregation are shown to be related to reported financial performance relationships. The study offers practical recommendations for improving rigor and transparency in corporate sustainability research. The second study examines how job applicants price corporate sustainability signals as part of their compensation using a choice-based conjoint experiment (N = 249) analyzed via Hierarchical Bayes. Drawing on Herzberg's hygiene-motivator distinction, the study finds two distinct asymmetries. Within domains, penalties for withdrawal exceed rewards for proactive investment. Across domains, climate commitments tied to managerial incentives generate a reliable compensation discount while equivalently structured diversity commitments do not. These patterns are consistent with diversity functioning as hygiene factor and climate functioning as prestige motivators. The third study employs a randomized between-subjects survey experiment with 516 retail investors to examine whether financial or impact framing of corporate sustainability strategies shifts investor sustainability judgments. Despite perceiving financial framing, retail investors showed no meaningful differences in perceived importance ratings or investor materiality assessments across framing conditions. Political ideology emerged as the dominant predictor of sustainability importance judgments and the strongest covariate predictor of investor materiality assessments, replicating across three independent samples. The findings challenge the assumption embedded in global disclosure frameworks that strategic framing shapes how retail investors receive sustainability information. Across three audiences and three methods, the dissertation finds that sustainability information does not operate uniformly. Its usefulness depends on who receives it, how it is disaggregated, and what psychological register it activates. These findings carry direct implications for how sustainability measures are constructed, disclosed, and regulated.

works.title: Choice and goal framing effects in food evaluation: The roles of positive–negative asymmetry and decision sequence
works.abstract: Food choices in everyday life are typically made as a sequence of repeated decisions rather than as isolated choices. We previously developed a sequential preference-based task and demonstrated consistent effects of choice framing on food choice behavior. Building upon that, the present study investigated two forms of framing: choice framing, by comparing Binary and Defer tasks, and goal framing, by contrasting Positive- and Negative-selection instructions. Participants completed a virtual food-shopping task in which food images were presented sequentially and each item was either accepted (“Take”), rejected (“Leave”), or, in some tasks, temporarily postponed (“Wait”). To characterize stage-specific and temporal dynamics of food choice, both aggregate and sequential analyses were conducted. Aggregate analyses replicated previous findings that “Take” decisions required longer processing times in both image viewing and evaluation stages than “Leave” decisions, whereas the “Wait” decision elicited the longest processing times, reflecting greater decision uncertainty. Furthermore, Negative-selection tasks elicited a reversed trend in different decision stages and higher between-participant variability for “Wait” decisions compared to Positive-selection tasks, despite identical task structures, supporting theories of positive–negative asymmetry. Sequential analyses further showed that response dynamics systematically evolved across Choice Sequences in Positive-selection tasks, whereas such temporal modulation was largely absent under Negative-selection, suggesting sustained cognitive demand throughout the task. These findings demonstrate that food choice is a dynamic, multi-stage process and illustrate how integrating stage-specific and sequential analyses can reveal cognitive mechanisms that remain hidden in conventional aggregate analyses. The present study highlights the value of integrating stage-specific and sequential analyses to advance understanding of consumer food decision-making.

works.title: Psychological effects of temporal landmarks: A meta-analysis of affective, cognitive, and self-regulatory processes
works.abstract: Temporal landmarks, distinct time points that may shape affect, cognition, and self-regulatory behavior, have effects whose magnitude and boundaries remain uncertain. This meta-analysis systematically synthesized findings on the psychological outcomes linked to temporal landmarks in consumption and decision-making contexts. Following a comprehensive literature search and screening, 31 studies with 83 effect sizes (total N = 13,765) were included, encompassing experimental, quasi-experimental, and cross-sectional designs. The primary three-level random-effects model with study-clustered CR2 inference indicated a small positive average effect (g = 0.332, 95% CI [0.050, 0.614], p = 0.023). High heterogeneity (I2 = 90.8%) indicates that this pooled estimate is a context-dependent average tendency rather than a stable or broadly generalizable effect. Excluding nine studies with methodological concerns yielded a similar positive estimate (g = 0.395). Beginning and special-event temporal landmarks had positive subgroup averages, whereas the effect of ending temporal landmarks was uncertain. Longer time spans were stronger only in unadjusted analyses, and cultural moderation appeared only in a small subset of special-event effects; neither pattern was robust in multivariate meta-regression. These findings support a cautious psychological account centered on temporal cognition, self-representation, and goal regulation.

works.title: Replication: Beyond gains and losses by Mishra and Fiddick (2012)
works.abstract: The standard framing effect demonstrates a deviation from expected utility theory (and rational choice theory) that is consistent with prospect theory. Findings by Mishra and Fiddick (2012) suggest that such framing effects may be better explained in terms of a sensitivity to minimal acceptable thresholds, or needs, as described in risk-sensitivity theory. To evaluate the reliability of the findings reported by Mishra and Fiddick (2012), we conducted a close preregistered replication of their Experiment 3 with a larger, well-powered sample ( N = 399) of UK students recruited via Prolific. Our results partly replicated the original findings: In line with the original study, we observed the standard framing effect and that individuals with higher need more often selected the risky option. Results for the crucial hypothesis were mixed: In the original study, the framing effect disappeared when the analysis stratified by need. In the replication, when we stratified by need, we observed a framing effect among participants with low need, but not among participants with high need. These findings contribute to the understanding of both prospect theory and risk-sensitivity theory in explaining the standard framing effect.

works.title: Trust in the police: understanding ethnic minority and majority differences through the multidimensional Intergroup Trust Model
works.abstract: Understanding trust between communities and police remains a critical societal challenge, particularly for ethnic minorities who consistently show lower police trust. This study applied the Intergroup Trust Model (IGT-Model), which conceptualizes trust as five-dimensional, to examine police trust variations between ethnic minority and majority members in two USA and New Zealand community samples. Study 1 (Boston) collected 252 surveys from three diverse neighborhoods (136 Black and 116 White residents). ANCOVAs revealed significant trust differences between groups. Hierarchical regression showed that Black participants' lower trust was primarily explained by a lack of compassion-, compatibility-, and security-based trust, whereas White participants' trust was predicted by integrity-based trust. Study 2 (Auckland) collected 331 surveys across three diverse neighborhoods (170 Māori, 161 White New Zealanders). ANCOVAs replicated significant trust differences between minority and majority groups. Hierarchical regression showed similar patterns: Māori lower trust was driven by lack of compassion- and compatibility-based trust, while White New Zealanders' trust was based on competence- and compassion-based trust. These findings indicate one-size-fits-all policing approaches cannot build genuine community trust. The IGT-Model provides a useful framework for unpacking complex trust compositions and designing targeted interventions. Recognizing trust's multidimensional nature allows nuanced strategies to rebuild police-community relationships and address historical disparities.

works.title: Knowledge and beliefs about behavioral biases
works.venue: Journal of Behavioral and Experimental Finance
works.abstract: We study knowledge and beliefs about ten behavioral biases in pre-registered online experiments with 1807 participants from relevant groups in society—i.e., general population, financial professionals, and behavioral scientists. The general population is broadly aware of the content of the biases, with 64% of statements assessed in line with scientific consensus. Behavioral scientists exhibit the highest knowledge, followed by financial professionals and the general population. Beliefs about groups’ modal answers exceed chance, and each group is best predicted by its own members. Furthermore, we document a pronounced agreement bias: measured knowledge is substantially lower when respondents must disagree with an incorrect statement than agree with a correct one. Finally, we conceptually replicate the bias blind spot: participants rate themselves less susceptible than the average person in their peer group for every bias. Moreover, they expect behavioral scientists to be the least and the general population the most prone to biases. Given the well-documented prevalence of behavioral biases across populations with varying levels of education and training in this area, our findings cast doubt on whether knowledge alone is an adequate channel for addressing these biases.

works.title: Un diario settimanale strutturato come intervento metacognitivo nella matematica del primo anno di ingegneria
works.abstract: First-year engineering students often struggle with university mathematics not for lack of effort, but for limited metacognitive awareness and self-regulatory skills. This quasi-experimental longitudinal study examines whether engagement with a structured weekly reflective diary predicts first-session examination success in Mathematical Analysis I, and whether this association is better explained by metacognitive and affective indicators than by study time alone. The diary was implemented via Moodle across two consecutive academic years at Politecnico di Torino, involving 228 and 215 first-time enrolment engineering students respectively. Each week, students reflected on study practices, perceived learning quality, emotional states, and resource use. Diary data were integrated with formative assessment scores and summative examination outcomes. Both cohorts showed a replicated dose-response relationship between diary engagement and first-session success. Pass rates rose from 22.2% and 7.7% among non-compilers to 62.6% and 78.5% among students completing 12–14 entries. Each additional completed diary was associated with 18% and 29% higher odds of success respectively, independent of formative assessment performance. A threshold effect emerged at approximately eight completed entries. Study hours did not predict grade in either cohort; self-assessed learning quality, self-evaluation frequency, and affective balance were consistent predictors. Early diary engagement distinguished successful from struggling students by week 4, supporting its use as a scalable early warning indicator. These findings suggest that structured reflective practice supports academic success through metacognitive and affective pathways. The diary system represents a low-cost, replicable intervention applicable across first-year university courses with structured weekly progressions.

works.title: THE PANCHADI LEARNING STEPS IN THE MODERN TEACHING CLASSROOM: A REVIEW OF NCF-SE 2023, TRADITIONAL INDIAN PEDAGOGY AND CONTEMPORARY EVIDENCE
works.venue: EPRA International Journal of Multidisciplinary Research (IJMR)
works.abstract: Modern classrooms are increasingly expected to move beyond traditional lecture-centred approaches towards more learner-centred and outcome-based forms of teaching, as highlighted in India’s National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 and the National Curriculum Framework for School Education (NCF-SE) 2023. In this changing educational landscape, traditional Indian pedagogical practices offer valuable insights into structured and sequential learning, although their potential application in contemporary instructional design has received relatively limited attention. Against this background, the present study examines the Panchadi learning steps, the five-step learning process recommended in the National Curriculum Framework (NCF-FS 2022, integrated within NCF-SE 2023) as a way for teachers to plan the sequence of classroom activities, and explores its conceptual foundations and its relevance to contemporary educational research. The study adopts a narrative review approach, drawing upon NCF policy documents, classical Indian pedagogical texts, foundational theories of learning, and major meta-analyses and research syntheses related to instructional effectiveness. Relevant literature was identified and examined on the basis of its conceptual contribution and methodological significance, followed by thematic organisation and analysis. Although the review does not adopt a PRISMA-based systematic review methodology, selected reporting principles from PRISMA 2020 were considered to improve transparency in the review process. The Panchadi framework, as set out in the NCF, consists of five interconnected steps: Aditi (introduction and connection with prior knowledge), Bodha (conceptual understanding), Abhyāsa (practice), Prayoga (application), and Prasāra (expansion through sharing and communicating learning). The review suggests that these steps share meaningful conceptual connections with several established evidence-based instructional practices, particularly active learning (Freeman et al., 2014; Hake, 1998), retrieval practice (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006), learning by explaining and teaching others (Fiorella & Mayer, 2013), formative assessment and feedback (Black & Wiliam, 1998; Hattie & Timperley, 2007), as well as the 5E and Herbartian instructional models and the classical Indian sequence of śravaṇa, manana and nididhyāsana. Overall, the Panchadi sequence emerges as a culturally rooted and theoretically coherent pedagogical framework with potential applications in contemporary classrooms, including blended and technology-supported learning environments. Nevertheless, the NCF describes Panchadi within its Foundational Stage framework and as a non-binding recommendation, and its actual contribution to teaching and learning outcomes, including at later school stages, needs to be established through further empirical investigation, particularly controlled classroom studies examining its influence on students’ academic achievement, learning engagement, and long-term knowledge retention.

works.title: Active Learning with Generative AI in Introductory Physics: A Multi-Institutional Study of the P-A.I.R. Framework
works.abstract: Generative AI tools have become part of how students study physics, yet unstructured use may reduce students' opportunities to work through problems independently. The Physics AI-Replication (P-A.I.R.) framework structures AI use as a four-step cycle: students identify a challenging problem, obtain an AI-generated explanation and solution, request similar practice problems, and solve them independently before reviewing the AI's solutions. We evaluated P-A.I.R. in 11 algebra- and calculus-based introductory physics sections at four U.S. institutions using a common end-of-semester survey. Most students reported improved conceptual understanding (90.9\%) and found the replicated practice problems helpful (97.7\%), and these two ratings were strongly associated ($r_s = 0.58$). Perceptions of both components, as well as post-engagement confidence ($μ= 7.18$ on a 1-10 scale), were consistent across institutions. Post-engagement confidence was associated with perceived improvement in conceptual understanding ($r_s = 0.37$) and the helpfulness of replicated practice ($r_s = 0.35$), but not with how often students used AI ($r_s = 0.02$) or with self-reported GPA ($r_s = 0.13$). Thematic analysis of open-ended responses showed that students valued AI primarily for conceptual clarification and structured problem solving (63.0\%), while their main concerns were AI accuracy (34.2\%) and the need for explanations that guide rather than simply provide answers (29.7\%). These findings suggest that how students engage with AI matters more than how often they use it, and that frameworks sequencing AI assistance with independent problem solving offer a practical, transferable approach for physics instruction.

works.title: CassLab: An interactive simulator for learning apache cassandra distributed mechanisms
works.abstract: Apache Cassandra is a widely adopted distributed NoSQL database whose internal mechanisms, including partitioning, replication, consistency management, and fault tolerance, can be difficult for students to understand using conventional learning resources. This paper presents CassLab , an interactive web-based educational simulator that enables learners to explore Cassandra’s distributed architecture without installing software, deploying servers or running a database cluster. Implemented as a client-side application, CassLab allows users to configure distributed clusters, analyze CQL table definitions, visualize partitioning and replica placement, simulate read and write execution paths, and explore virtual nodes, failure scenarios, consistency evaluation, and cluster rebalancing through interactive animations. The simulation engine was validated against a physical Apache Cassandra 5.0 cluster: tokens, replica sets, primary replicas and consistency outcomes under failure conditions agreed in all test cases for the deterministic mechanisms it covers. In a matched pre/post classroom study with 51 engineering students, the mean score on an objective knowledge test rose from 4.73 to 7.24 out of 12 between a conventional lecture and the end of a one-week period that included access to CassLab and one guided laboratory session, and students rated its usability highly (mean SUS score 81.7). Without a control group, this gain cannot be attributed to CassLab alone: repeated testing and other learning activities may have contributed. Perceived difficulty also increased, potentially because students had initially overestimated their understanding. These findings suggest that CassLab can be used as a complementary instructional resource alongside documentation and database administration tools for teaching Apache Cassandra.

works.title: Pre-AI Sensemaking Before Scale: How Somagraphic Learning™ Puts Human Cognition Back in the Driver's Seat
works.venue: Illinois Digital Environment for Access to Learning and Scholarship (University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign)
works.abstract: The consequential question about AI in learning is not whether it belongs, but when it enters. AI answers arrive in seconds, worded precisely to match what the user asked. When users/learners have not yet formed their own understanding, they have nothing to push back against, and AI’s explanation becomes their first encounter with the idea. This is the timing problem, not an AI problem. This chapter introduces Somagraphic Learning™, a human-first visual-cognitive framework built around a fixed three-stage sequence: Attempt → Map → Refine. Learners externalize what they already think using hands and simple shapes, articulate at least one clear relationship ([Concept A] affects [Concept B] because [Reason]), and identify the specific gap in their understanding. AI enters only at the Refine stage, through a gap-based query rather than a generation-based one. Shape-Emotion Grammar™ (Shape → Motion → Emotion → Meaning) supports the Attempt and Map stages as a pre-verbal visual grammar. Shapes, spatial arrangements and motion cues need no English proficiency, so multilingual learners can think in any language or symbol before AI enters. Somatic AI Literacy™ is proposed as a competency domain: the capacity to establish embodied conceptual orientation before AI interaction begins. The Map Before Machine™ card applies Body-to-Screen Cognition as a 5-minute, analog-first thinking tool in three delivery formats: printable, LMS-integrated, and embedded onboarding within AI platforms. The chapter examines five global challenges to equity and inclusion: language equity for multilingual learners and non-native English writers, low-resource classrooms where the analog stages need no connectivity, access in tooling, the policy vacuum in high-investment markets, and cognitive sovereignty in the workforce. It applies Universal Design for Learning’s multiple means of representation at the pre-interaction stage. Three practice contexts (USA, UAE, Oman) show the sequence in use. The Somagraphic diagram also serves as a time-stamped, learner-generated artifact that predates any AI output. The framework is theoretically grounded and not yet empirically validated at scale or across cultures, ages, genders and neurodivergent profiles. The chapter closes with a falsifiable research agenda, including cross-cultural replication in Arabic, Hindi, Mandarin and English-medium contexts, because the sequence is the hypothesis.
